sandhi.note: Before the unvoiced p the visarga stays. Compare नो देवि in the first line, where the next sound is voiced.
The s of the prefix निस् becomes visarga before the sibilant s of स्वन.

samasa.literal: with the sound of the bell
samasa.sense: with the ringing of the bell that stunned the asuras in battle (2.56)

samasa.vigraha: चापस्य ज्या चापज्या; तस्याः निःस्वनः, तेन
samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (चापज्या)
samasa.literal: with the out-sound of the bow’s string
samasa.sense: with the twang of her bowstring
samasa.alt: निःस्वन is itself a prefixed noun, निस् + स्वन, ‘sound going out’, the resounding twang.

morph.note: Imperative 2nd sg. of √पा ‘protect’ (adādi class): पा + हि. Said three times in the verse.
Enclitic acc. pl. of अस्मद्, used in place of अस्मान्. As an enclitic it never begins a sentence; here it follows पाहि and घण्टास्वनेन.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) देवि, शूलेन नः पाहि; (हे) अम्बिके, खड्गेन च (नः) पाहि; घण्टास्वनेन चापज्यानिःस्वनेन च नः पाहि।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three imperatives (पाहि) with one object (नः) and four instruments: trident, sword, the bell’s sound, the bowstring’s twang.
mantras.lit: With the trident protect us, O Devī; protect (us) with the sword too, O Ambikā; with the sound of the bell protect us, and with the twang of the bowstring.
mantras.tr: Protect us with your trident, O Devī; protect us with your sword, O Mother; protect us with the ringing of your bell and the twang of your bowstring.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Your’ is supplied throughout: these are the weapons the gods gave her in 2.20–24.

comm.t: The hymn changes metre and mood: from the long vasantatilakā praises the gods turn to a short anuṣṭubh prayer for protection. Four of her attributes are invoked: trident, sword, bell and bow, each a god’s gift in 2.20–24 (Śiva’s trident, Vāyu’s bow, Indra’s bell from Airāvata, Kāla’s sword).

Even the sounds of her weapons protect: the bell, whose ringing stunned the asuras (घण्टास्वनविमोहितान्, 2.56), and the bowstring, whose twang shook the worlds (धनुर्ज्यानिःस्वनेन, 2.38). The four verses 4.24–27 are often recited on their own as a prayer for protection.

sandhi_exceptions.reason: The vowels stand apart at the pāda break (भ्रामणेनात्मशूलस्य | उत्तरस्यां): epic and Purāṇic verse often leaves sandhi unapplied between the third and fourth pādas, and joining them (…शूलस्योत्तरस्यां) would take a syllable from the half-line, leaving seven where the metre needs eight. A metrical licence, printed so in the Gita Press text.

morph.note: The other three quarters are feminine locatives (प्राच्याम्, प्रतीच्याम्, उत्तरस्याम्, with दिशि understood). The south is named with the m./n. locative of दक्षिण, ‘on the southern side’; the feminine would be दक्षिणस्याम्.
उत्तर in the sense of a direction is declined like a pronoun: feminine loc. sg. -स्याम् (as सर्वस्याम्).
Action noun from the causative of √भ्रम्: ‘by causing to whirl’, the trident swung round about.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) चण्डिके, प्राच्यां (नः) रक्ष, प्रतीच्यां च (रक्ष), दक्षिणे रक्ष; तथा (हे) ईश्वरि, आत्मशूलस्य भ्रामणेन उत्तरस्यां (रक्ष)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A series of imperatives with ‘us’ understood from 4.24. The instrumental भ्रामणेनात्मशूलस्य can go with the north alone or, through तथा ‘likewise’, with all four quarters.
mantras.lit: In the east protect (us), and in the west; O Caṇḍikā, protect (us) in the south; by the whirling of your own trident, likewise in the north, O Īśvarī.
mantras.tr: Protect us in the east and in the west, O Caṇḍikā; protect us in the south; and in the north as well, O Sovereign Lady, by the whirling of your trident.

comm.t: The prayer now covers space: the four quarters are named one by one, and her own trident, whirled about her, is the guard.

Guarding the quarters is the usual plan of protective prayers (kavacas), in which each direction is given a guardian; the Devī Kavaca recited before the Saptaśatī in the Gita Press pāṭha follows that plan. Here one Goddess guards them all.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name चण्डिका (755), the name by which the Devī Māhātmya addresses her here and throughout. The shared name belongs to a shared Śākta vocabulary; the works are separate.

sandhi.note: a + a → ā; inside the compound अति + अर्थ → अत्यर्थ (i before a vowel becomes y).
The visarga of तैः (as r) is dropped before the r of रक्ष. The rule lengthens the vowel before it, but ai is already long, so nothing more changes.

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (the first member, अत्यर्थ ‘beyond measure’, qualifies adverbially)
samasa.alt: अत्यर्थ is itself a prādi compound, अर्थम् अतिक्रान्तम्, ‘passing the measure’.

morph.note: Taddhita from सोम (the moon, or Soma): ‘moon-like’, hence mild, gentle; the opposite of घोर.
The correlative of both relative clauses (यानि … यानि च …): ‘with those (forms)’.
Accusative singular of the feminine root-noun भू ‘earth’.

mantras.anvaya: यानि ते सौम्यानि रूपाणि त्रैलोक्ये विचरन्ति, यानि च अत्यर्थघोराणि (रूपाणि त्रैलोक्ये विचरन्ति), तैः अस्मान् तथा भुवं रक्ष।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two relative clauses (यानि … यानि च …) taken up by one correlative (तैः), then the imperative with two objects.
mantras.lit: Your gentle forms which move about in the three worlds, and those which are terrible beyond measure — with them protect us and the earth as well.
mantras.tr: With all your forms that roam the three worlds, the gentle ones and those terrible beyond measure, protect us, and the earth as well.

comm.t: After the quarters of space, the forms of the Goddess: her gentle forms and her terrible ones alike are asked to guard the gods and the earth.

The pairing of gentle (सौम्य) and terrible (घोर) forms is basic to Śākta thought; both are hers, and both protect. The hymn has shown both: the moon-like face of 4.12 and 4.20 and the face of wrath in 4.13.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) includes the name सौम्या (910), ‘the gentle one’. The Devī Māhātmya asks for the protection of the gentle and the terrible forms together.

samasa.vigraha: खड्गः च शूलं च गदा च खड्गशूलगदाः; ताः आदौ येषां तानि
samasa.type: bahuvrīhi with आदि, whose first member is an itaretara dvandva
samasa.literal: having sword, trident and mace at their head
samasa.sense: the sword, the trident, the mace and all the rest

samasa.vigraha: करः पल्लवः इव करपल्लवः; करपल्लवेषु सङ्गीनि
samasa.type: saptamī tatpuruṣa whose first member is a karmadhāraya of comparison (करपल्लव, with the standard of comparison पल्लव placed second)
samasa.sense: held in her soft, leaf-tender hands
samasa.alt: करपल्लव can also be read as a metaphor, ‘the hand that is a tender shoot’ (करः एव पल्लवः); the meaning is the same.

morph.note: The last member सङ्गिन् (√सञ्ज् ‘cling’ + -इन्) is declined as a neuter -इन् stem: nom. pl. -ईनि.
सर्व + the suffix -तस्, ‘from all sides’, hence ‘on every side’.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) अम्बिके, खड्गशूलगदादीनि करपल्लवसङ्गीनि यानि च ते अस्त्राणि (सन्ति), तैः अस्मान् सर्वतः रक्ष।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (यानि … अस्त्राणि) taken up by the correlative तैः; the imperative रक्ष ends the hymn’s petitions.
mantras.lit: And your weapons, O Ambikā — sword, trident, mace and the rest — which cling to your sprout-like hands: with them protect us on every side.
mantras.tr: And with all your weapons, O Mother — sword, trident, mace and the rest — that rest in your tender hands, protect us on every side.

comm.t: The last petition of the hymn: all her weapons, held in her soft hands, are asked to guard the gods from every side. It completes the prayer begun in 4.24 with trident and sword.

Terrible weapons in leaf-tender hands repeat in small the hymn’s theme of the gentle and the fierce in one Goddess. With this verse the Śakrādi Stuti ends; the narrative resumes at 4.28, and the gods worship her with flowers and incense (4.29–30).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name शूलाद्यायुधसम्पन्ना (506), ‘endowed with the trident and other weapons’, built with the same ‘X and the rest’ (आदि) pattern as खड्गशूलगदादीनि. The works are separate.
